feed.title: Knot of the day · Knot Atlas
feed.subtitle: One knot a day from the Knot Atlas, with its steps.

entry.title: Double Sheet Bend
entry.summary: A sheet bend with a second turn of the thinner rope round the bight. Use it when the two ropes differ a lot in size, or when the rope is slippery.
entry.content:
A sheet bend with a second turn of the thinner rope round the bight. Use it when the two ropes differ a lot in size, or when the rope is slippery.

  1. Make a bight in the thicker rope (yellow).
  2. Bring the thinner rope (blue) up through the bight from behind.
  3. Take it round behind both legs of the bight, then round a second time beside the first turn.
  4. Bring it across the front and tuck it under itself both times, not into the bight.
  5. Hold the bight and pull the blue standing part to set the knot.

entry.title: Half Hitch
entry.summary: The simplest hitch: the end goes round the standing part and across itself. On its own it is not secure, but it is the building block of many hitches and the usual way to finish one.
entry.content:
The simplest hitch: the end goes round the standing part and across itself. On its own it is not secure, but it is the building block of many hitches and the usual way to finish one.

  1. Pass the end through the ring from front to back.
  2. Bring it down behind the standing part.
  3. Bring it round to the front of the standing part.
  4. Take it round the standing part and across over itself.
  5. Pull the end snug against the standing part.

entry.title: Three-Strand Flat Braid
entry.summary: A flat braid of 3 strands. Alternately from the left and the right, the outermost strand is brought to the middle, passing over and under the strands on its way.
entry.content:
A flat braid of 3 strands. Alternately from the left and the right, the outermost strand is brought to the middle, passing over and under the strands on its way.

  1. Bind the strands together at the top and spread them flat. Bring the outer left strand to the middle, over-under the strands it passes.
  2. Now the outer right strand to the middle, the same way. Then left again, then right.
  3. Carry on alternating. Pull each strand snug as it reaches the middle.
  4. Bind the strands together at the end.

entry.title: Round Turn and Two Half Hitches
entry.summary: A round turn on a ring or post takes the load while you finish with two half hitches round the standing part. It is secure, and it can be untied even with the rope under strain.
entry.content:
A round turn on a ring or post takes the load while you finish with two half hitches round the standing part. It is secure, and it can be untied even with the rope under strain.

  1. Pass the end through the ring from front to back.
  2. Pass it through again, so the rope makes a full round turn on the ring.
  3. Bring the end down behind the standing part and round to the front.
  4. First half hitch: take the end round the standing part and across over itself.
  5. Second half hitch, the same way, below the first. Tuck the end under.
  6. Slide the half hitches up toward the ring and pull them snug.

entry.title: Surgeon’s Knot
entry.summary: A square knot with an extra twist in the first half. The double twist grips while you tie the second half, so the knot does not loosen in between.
entry.content:
A square knot with an extra twist in the first half. The double twist grips while you tie the second half, so the knot does not loosen in between.

  1. Cross the two ends and twist them round each other twice.
  2. Pull the double twist snug: it holds by itself.
  3. Cross the ends the opposite way and twist them once.
  4. Pull all four ends to tighten.

entry.title: Seven-Strand Flat Braid
entry.summary: A flat braid of 7 strands. Alternately from the left and the right, the outermost strand is brought to the middle, passing over and under the strands on its way.
entry.content:
A flat braid of 7 strands. Alternately from the left and the right, the outermost strand is brought to the middle, passing over and under the strands on its way.

  1. Bind the strands together at the top and spread them flat. Bring the outer left strand to the middle, over-under the strands it passes.
  2. Now the outer right strand to the middle, the same way. Then left again, then right.

  4. Bind the strands together at the end.

entry.title: Sheet Bend
entry.summary: The everyday knot for joining two ropes, including ropes of different thickness. The thicker or stiffer rope makes the bight; the thinner one wraps round it.
entry.content:
The everyday knot for joining two ropes, including ropes of different thickness. The thicker or stiffer rope makes the bight; the thinner one wraps round it.

  1. Make a bight in the thicker rope (yellow).
  2. Bring the thinner rope (blue) up through the bight from behind.
  3. Take it round behind both legs of the bight.
  4. Bring it across the front and tuck it under itself, not into the bight.
  5. Hold the bight and pull the blue standing part to set the knot.

entry.title: Surgeon’s Knot with Second Tuck
entry.summary: The surgeon’s knot with the extra twist in both halves. It is bulkier, but grips better still in slippery line.
entry.content:
The surgeon’s knot with the extra twist in both halves. It is bulkier, but grips better still in slippery line.

  1. Cross the two ends and twist them round each other twice.
  2. Pull the double twist snug.
  3. Cross the ends the opposite way and twist them twice again.
  4. Pull all four ends to tighten.

entry.title: Turk’s Head (4 lead, 5 bight)
entry.summary: A woven band round a pole or rail. Followed round, the single rope crosses itself in a strict over-under pattern: 4 strands lie side by side all the way round (the leads) and the band has 5 scallops on each edge (the bights).
entry.content:
A woven band round a pole or rail. Followed round, the single rope crosses itself in a strict over-under pattern: 4 strands lie side by side all the way round (the leads) and the band has 5 scallops on each edge (the bights).

  1. Wrap the rope round the pole, starting the pattern: each time it meets another part of itself it goes over, then under, then over.
  2. Keep following the pattern round. Rotate the pole as you go, so you always work on the front.
  3. Keep the over-under strict. One wrong crossing changes the knot.
  4. When the end meets the start, the band is complete. Lay the end alongside the start to follow the pattern round again.
  5. Tighten gradually all round and tuck the ends under the band.

entry.title: Round Turn and Two Half Hitches
entry.summary: A round turn on a ring or post takes the load while you finish with two half hitches round the standing part. It is secure, and it can be untied even with the rope under strain.
entry.content:
A round turn on a ring or post takes the load while you finish with two half hitches round the standing part. It is secure, and it can be untied even with the rope under strain.

  1. Pass the end through the ring from front to back.
  2. Pass it through again, so the rope makes a full round turn on the ring.
  3. Bring the end down behind the standing part and round to the front.
  4. First half hitch: take the end round the standing part and across over itself.
  5. Second half hitch, the same way, below the first. Tuck the end under.
  6. Slide the half hitches up toward the ring and pull them snug.

entry.title: Two Half Hitches
entry.summary: A turn through a ring or round a post, then two half hitches round the standing part, both the same way. Together the half hitches form a clove hitch on the standing part.
entry.content:
A turn through a ring or round a post, then two half hitches round the standing part, both the same way. Together the half hitches form a clove hitch on the standing part.

  1. Pass the end through the ring from front to back.
  2. Bring it down behind the standing part.
  3. Bring it round to the front.
  4. First half hitch: round the standing part and across over itself.
  5. Second half hitch, the same way, below the first. Tuck the end under.
  6. Slide the hitches up to the ring and pull them snug.

entry.title: Italian Hitch
entry.summary: A hitch on a carabiner or bar that lets rope run under control. Both strands leave on the same side of the bar, and the rope rubs on itself and the bar. It reverses neatly: pull the other strand and the hitch flips through the bar and runs the other way.
entry.content:
A hitch on a carabiner or bar that lets rope run under control. Both strands leave on the same side of the bar, and the rope rubs on itself and the bar. It reverses neatly: pull the other strand and the hitch flips through the bar and runs the other way.

  1. The loaded strand comes up to the bar.
  2. Take it over the bar and round, as for a cow hitch.
  3. Bring it across the front, over one leg and under the other.
  4. Round the bar again: both strands now leave on the same side.
  5. Hold the free strand to control the rope as it runs round the bar.

entry.summary: A flat braid of 7 strands. Alternately from the left and the right, the outermost strand is brought to the middle, passing over and under the strands on its way.

entry.title: Two Half Hitches
entry.summary: A turn through a ring or round a post, then two half hitches round the standing part, both the same way. Together the half hitches form a clove hitch on the standing part.
entry.content:
A turn through a ring or round a post, then two half hitches round the standing part, both the same way. Together the half hitches form a clove hitch on the standing part.

  1. Pass the end through the ring from front to back.
  2. Bring it down behind the standing part.
  3. Bring it round to the front.
  4. First half hitch: round the standing part and across over itself.
  5. Second half hitch, the same way, below the first. Tuck the end under.
  6. Slide the hitches up to the ring and pull them snug.

entry.title: Constrictor Knot
entry.summary: A clove hitch with an extra tuck, which locks the two ends under the crossing turn. It grips a round object so hard that it often has to be cut off.
entry.content:
A clove hitch with an extra tuck, which locks the two ends under the crossing turn. It grips a round object so hard that it often has to be cut off.

  1. Bring the working end across the front of the post.
  2. Take it round behind the post and back to the front, above the standing part.
  3. Cross it diagonally over the first turn and round behind the post again.
  4. Bring the end to the front, over the standing part and under the diagonal. The two ends now cross under it.
  5. Pull both ends hard. The diagonal clamps the crossing underneath it.

entry.title: Square Knot
entry.summary: A flat binding knot for tying the two ends of one cord round something: a parcel, a bandage, a reefed sail. It lies flat and comes undone easily. Here it is shown as two interlocked bights, one in each end, so you can see how it is built.
entry.content:
A flat binding knot for tying the two ends of one cord round something: a parcel, a bandage, a reefed sail. It lies flat and comes undone easily. Here it is shown as two interlocked bights, one in each end, so you can see how it is built.

  1. Make a bight in the left-hand end (yellow). Its short leg is the working end.
  2. Bring the blue end in from the right, over the curve of the yellow bight and under its lower leg.
  3. Take it round outside the narrow neck of the yellow bight, over both yellow legs.
  4. Bring it back under the upper yellow leg and out over the curve, beside its own standing part.
  5. Pull all four parts evenly. Both parts of each rope lie side by side and come out on the same side.

entry.title: Four-Strand Flat Braid
entry.summary: A flat braid of 4 strands. Alternately from the left and the right, the outermost strand is brought to the middle, passing over and under the strands on its way.
entry.content:
A flat braid of 4 strands. Alternately from the left and the right, the outermost strand is brought to the middle, passing over and under the strands on its way.

  1. Bind the strands together at the top and spread them flat. Bring the outer left strand to the middle, over-under the strands it passes.
  2. Now the outer right strand to the middle, the same way. Then left again, then right.
  3. Carry on alternating. Pull each strand snug as it reaches the middle.
  4. Bind the strands together at the end.

entry.title: Sheer Lashing
entry.summary: Lashes two poles side by side, to lengthen a pole or to make sheer legs (an A-frame). Start with a clove hitch, wrap round both poles, tighten with frapping turns between them, finish with a clove hitch.
entry.content:
Lashes two poles side by side, to lengthen a pole or to make sheer legs (an A-frame). Start with a clove hitch, wrap round both poles, tighten with frapping turns between them, finish with a clove hitch.

  1. Tie a clove hitch round one pole.
  2. Wrap the rope round both poles, six or more turns, working along them. Keep the turns snug and side by side.
  3. Take two frapping turns between the poles, round the lashing turns, and pull them hard.
  4. Finish with a clove hitch round the other pole.
  5. Check that the poles cannot slide against each other.

entry.title: Improved Clinch Knot
entry.summary: A clinch knot with one extra tuck: after going through the small loop by the eye, the end goes back through the big loop it has just made. The tuck stops the knot slipping in thin or slippery line.
entry.content:
A clinch knot with one extra tuck: after going through the small loop by the eye, the end goes back through the big loop it has just made. The tuck stops the knot slipping in thin or slippery line.

  1. Pass the end of the line through the eye of the hook.
  2. Bring it back up alongside the line.
  3. Twist the end round the line five times, working away from the hook.
  4. Bring the end back down and through the small loop just above the eye.
  5. Then tuck it back through the big loop you have just made.
  6. Wet it and pull the line steadily so the twists close onto the eye. Trim the end.

entry.title: Figure-Eight Knot
entry.summary: The standard stopper. It is bulkier than the Overhand, harder to pull through a hole, and it can usually be undone even after a heavy load. Its shape makes it easy to check at a glance.
entry.content:
The standard stopper. It is bulkier than the Overhand, harder to pull through a hole, and it can usually be undone even after a heavy load. Its shape makes it easy to check at a glance.

  1. Hold the standing part at the top. The working end hangs below and does all the moving.
  2. Bring the end up and across the standing part to make a loop.
  3. Carry the end on round, behind the standing part.
  4. Bring it back down through the first loop.
  5. Pull the end and the standing part apart to draw the knot into its figure-eight shape.

entry.title: Two Half Hitches
entry.summary: A turn through a ring or round a post, then two half hitches round the standing part, both the same way. Together the half hitches form a clove hitch on the standing part.
entry.content:
A turn through a ring or round a post, then two half hitches round the standing part, both the same way. Together the half hitches form a clove hitch on the standing part.

  1. Pass the end through the ring from front to back.
  2. Bring it down behind the standing part.
  3. Bring it round to the front.
  4. First half hitch: round the standing part and across over itself.
  5. Second half hitch, the same way, below the first. Tuck the end under.
  6. Slide the hitches up to the ring and pull them snug.

entry.title: Figure-Eight Loop
entry.summary: A Figure-Eight Knot tied in a doubled rope. It makes a strong fixed eye that is easy to check by eye, which is why climbers use it.
entry.content:
A Figure-Eight Knot tied in a doubled rope. It makes a strong fixed eye that is easy to check by eye, which is why climbers use it.

  1. Double the end of the rope into a long bight. You tie with the doubled rope.
  2. Bring the bight up and across the doubled standing part to make a loop.
  3. Carry it on round, behind the standing part.
  4. Bring it back down through the first loop.
  5. Pull the bight through to make the eye. Dress every strand so it runs parallel.
  6. Hold the eye and pull each of the four strands in turn to set the knot.

entry.title: Surgeon’s Knot
entry.summary: A square knot with an extra twist in the first half. The double twist grips while you tie the second half, so the knot does not loosen in between.
entry.content:
A square knot with an extra twist in the first half. The double twist grips while you tie the second half, so the knot does not loosen in between.

  1. Cross the two ends and twist them round each other twice.
  2. Pull the double twist snug: it holds by itself.
  3. Cross the ends the opposite way and twist them once.
  4. Pull all four ends to tighten.

entry.title: Bowline with Stopper
entry.summary: A bowline with its tail tied in an overhand knot round the leg of the eye beside it, so the bowline cannot shake loose when it is not loaded.
entry.content:
A bowline with its tail tied in an overhand knot round the leg of the eye beside it, so the bowline cannot shake loose when it is not loaded.

  1. Tie a bowline: the standing part runs up.
  2. Make the small loop.
  3. Form the eye.
  4. Up through the small loop.
  5. Round behind the standing part.
  6. Back down through the small loop.
  7. Take the tail round the leg of the eye beside it and tie an overhand knot.
  8. Pull the overhand snug up against the bowline.

entry.title: Common Whipping
entry.summary: Turns of thin twine bound round a rope end to stop it unravelling. Both ends of the twine are buried under the turns.
entry.content:
Turns of thin twine bound round a rope end to stop it unravelling. Both ends of the twine are buried under the turns.

  1. Lay a bight of twine along the rope, with the loop pointing to the end of the rope.
  2. Wrap the twine round the rope and over the bight, working toward the end. Pull each turn tight.
  3. Pass the end through the loop of the bight.
  4. Pull the other end of the twine to draw the loop and the end under the turns. Trim both ends.

entry.title: Round Turn and Two Half Hitches
entry.summary: A round turn on a ring or post takes the load while you finish with two half hitches round the standing part. It is secure, and it can be untied even with the rope under strain.
entry.content:
A round turn on a ring or post takes the load while you finish with two half hitches round the standing part. It is secure, and it can be untied even with the rope under strain.

  1. Pass the end through the ring from front to back.
  2. Pass it through again, so the rope makes a full round turn on the ring.
  3. Bring the end down behind the standing part and round to the front.
  4. First half hitch: take the end round the standing part and across over itself.
  5. Second half hitch, the same way, below the first. Tuck the end under.
  6. Slide the half hitches up toward the ring and pull them snug.

entry.title: Clove Hitch
entry.summary: Two turns round a post with the second crossing over the first. It is quick to tie, easy to adjust, and it starts most lashings.
entry.content:
Two turns round a post with the second crossing over the first. It is quick to tie, easy to adjust, and it starts most lashings.

  1. Bring the working end across the front of the post.
  2. Take it round behind the post and back to the front, above the standing part.
  3. Cross it diagonally over the first turn and round behind the post again.
  4. Bring the end round to the front and tuck it under the diagonal, so it leaves in the opposite direction to the standing part.
  5. Pull both ends to snug the turns against the post.

entry.title: Italian Hitch
entry.summary: A hitch on a carabiner or bar that lets rope run under control. Both strands leave on the same side of the bar, and the rope rubs on itself and the bar. It reverses neatly: pull the other strand and the hitch flips through the bar and runs the other way.
entry.content:
A hitch on a carabiner or bar that lets rope run under control. Both strands leave on the same side of the bar, and the rope rubs on itself and the bar. It reverses neatly: pull the other strand and the hitch flips through the bar and runs the other way.

  1. The loaded strand comes up to the bar.
  2. Take it over the bar and round, as for a cow hitch.
  3. Bring it across the front, over one leg and under the other.
  4. Round the bar again: both strands now leave on the same side.
  5. Hold the free strand to control the rope as it runs round the bar.

entry.title: Granny Knot
entry.summary: The square knot tied wrong: both halves twisted the same way. It is shown here so you can recognise it and retie it. It either slips or jams, and it sits twisted across the knot instead of lying flat.
entry.content:
The square knot tied wrong: both halves twisted the same way. It is shown here so you can recognise it and retie it. It either slips or jams, and it sits twisted across the knot instead of lying flat.

  1. Make a bight in the left-hand end (yellow).
  2. Bring the blue end in from the right, under the yellow curve and over the lower leg.
  3. Take it round the neck of the yellow bight: over one yellow leg and under the other.
  4. Bring it back out. Its two parts now come out on opposite faces of the yellow bight.
  5. Pulled tight, the knot twists across its own length instead of lying flat. That is the sign of a granny.

entry.title: Clinch Knot
entry.summary: The classic way to tie line to a hook, lure or swivel: through the eye, five twists round the line, then back through the small loop by the eye.
entry.content:
The classic way to tie line to a hook, lure or swivel: through the eye, five twists round the line, then back through the small loop by the eye.

  1. Pass the end of the line through the eye of the hook.
  2. Bring it back up alongside the line.
  3. Twist the end round the line five times, working away from the hook.
  4. Bring the end back down and through the small loop just above the eye.
  5. Wet it, then pull the line so the twists slide down onto the eye. Trim the end.
